title: Function, domain, codomain, range, and fixed point
terms: function; domain; codomain; range; image; fixed point; natural domain.

exposition.text:
A function f : A → B assigns exactly one element of B to each element of its domain A. The
target set B is the codomain; the actual range, or image, is f(A) = {f(x) : x ∈ A} ⊆ B.
The book sometimes uses “range” for the target set; distinguishing the two is essential when
testing surjectivity. The natural real domain of a formula excludes zero denominators, negative
radicands for even roots, and nonpositive logarithm arguments.
A fixed point is an input x with f(x) = x. It must belong to the domain and also be a possible
output. Algebraic manipulation of this equation can introduce extraneous roots, especially after
squaring or cancelling denominators. Domain analysis should precede algebra, and candidate
solutions should be checked in the original expression.

solution.text:
The radicand is nonnegative exactly on (−∞, −2) ∪ [1, ∞). The logarithm requires x ̸= 0,
and its appearance in the denominator also excludes x = ±1. Only 1 lies in the preliminary
domain, yielding the stated union.

For f(x) = 3x + 4 on its natural real domain, how many fixed points does f ◦ f have?
(A) 0 (B) 1 (C) 2 (D) 3 (E) 4

solution.text:
The function f is strictly increasing. If f(x) > x, then f(f(x)) > f(x) > x; if f(x) < x,

x = 4, −1 after squaring, but only x = 4 is nonnegative.

solution.text:

question.text:
2
For how many real values of a does f (x) = x + a have exactly one real fixed point?
(A) 1 (B) Infinitely many (C) 2 (D) 3 (E) 0

solution.text:
2
Fixed points solve x − x + a = 0. There is exactly one distinct real root precisely when 1 −
4a = 0, so only a = 1/4 works.
